pick.e: From Middle English piken, picken, pikken, from Old English *piccian, *pīcian (attested in pīcung (“a pricking”)), and pīcan, pȳcan (“to pick, prick, pluck”), both from Proto-West Germanic *pikkōn, from Proto-Germanic *pikkōną (“to pick, peck, prick, knock”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew-, *bu- (“to make a dull, hollow sound”).
pick.g: A tool used for digging; a pickaxe.

picture.e: From Middle English picture, from Latin pictūra (“the art of painting, a painting”), from pingō (“to paint”).
picture.g: A representation of anything (as a person, a landscape, a building) upon canvas, paper, or other surface, by drawing, painting, printing, ph

piece.e: From Middle English pece, peece, peice, from Old French piece, from Late Latin pecia, petia (“broken piece, fragment; parcel of land”), of uncertain origin. Possibly ultimately from Gaulish *pettyā, from Proto-Celtic *kʷezdis (“piece, portion, quota”).
piece.g: A part of a larger whole, usually in such a form that it is able to be separated from other parts.

pierce.e: From Middle English perce, from conjugated forms of Old French percier such as (jeo) pierce (“I pierce”), probably from Vulgar Latin *pertūsiō, from Latin pertūsus, past participle of pertundō (“thrust or bore through”), from per- (“through”) + tundō (“beat, pound”).
Borrowed from Japanese ピアス (piasu, “pierced earring”), itself from English pierce.

piercing.g: Appearing to look deeply into; penetrating.

piety.e: From Middle English piete, borrowed from Middle French pieté, from Latin pietās. By surface analysis, pious + -ety.

pig.e: From Middle English pigge (“pig, piglet”) (originally a term for a young pig, with adult pigs being swyn (“swine”)), from Old English *picga, *pycga (attested in picgbrēad (“mast, pig-fodder”)), perhaps a diminutive of Proto-West Germanic *puk, *pūk (“pig”), which also gave rise to Middle Low German pûke, puyke (“pig, piglet”).
pig.g: Any of several mammalian species of the family Suidae, having cloven hooves, bristles and a snout adapted for digging; especially the domest

pig.e: Possibly a transferred use of pig, because the vessel was thought to resemble the animal.

pigeon.e: From Middle English pygeoun, borrowed from Old French pyjon, inherited from Late Latin pīpiōnem (“chirping bird”), derived from Latin pīpiāre (“to chirp”), of imitative origin. Partly displaced native English dove.
pigeon.g: One of several birds of the family Columbidae within the order Columbiformes.

pigeon.e: From pidgin English, from a Chinese Pidgin English pronunciation of English business during trade in the Far East.

pile.e: From Middle English pyle, from Old French pile, from Latin pīla (“pillar, pier”).
pile.g: A mass of things heaped together; a heap.

pile.e: From Middle English pile, from Old English pīl, from Proto-West Germanic *pīl, from Latin pīlum (“heavy javelin”).

pilgrim.e: From Middle English pilegrim, from Old English pilegrī̆m, from Old French pelegrin, from Latin peregrīnus (“foreigner”). The change of /r…r/ to /l…r/ is an effect of dissimilation in early Romance; compare Italian pellegrino.
pilgrim.g: One who travels to visit a site of religious significance.

pilgrimage.e: From Middle English pilgrimage. By surface analysis, pilgrim + -age.
pilgrimage.g: A journey made to a sacred place, or a religious journey.

pill.e: From Middle English pille (also pillem), a borrowing from Middle Low German pille or Middle Dutch pille (whence Dutch pil), probably from Latin pila, pilula. (persuade or convince): Generalized from red pill.
pill.g: A small, usually round or cylindrical object designed for easy swallowing, usually containing some sort of medication.

pill.e: From Middle English pillen, pilen, from Old English pilian (“to peel”), from Latin pilō (“depilate”), from pilus (“hair”).
pill.g: To peel; to remove the outer layer of hair, skin, or bark.

pillage.e: From Old French pillage, from piller (“plunder”), from an unattested meaning of Late Latin piliō, probably a figurative use of Latin pilō (“to remove (hair)”), from pilus (“hair”).
pillage.g: To loot or plunder by force, especially in time of war.

pillar.e: From Middle English piler, from Old French pilier, from Medieval Latin or Vulgar Latin *pilāre (“a pillar”), from Latin pila (“a pillar, pier, mole”).
pillar.g: A large post, often used as supporting architecture.

pillow.e: From Middle English pilwe, from Old English pyle, pylu (“pillow”), from Proto-West Germanic *pulwī (“pillow”), from Latin pulvīnus (“cushion”), derived from pulvis (“dust”), for the filler of a pillow.
pillow.g: A soft cushion used to support the head in bed.

pilot.e: From Middle French pilot, pillot, from Italian pilota, piloto, older also pedotta, pedot(t)o (the form in pil- is probably influenced by pileggiare (“to sail, navigate”)); ultimately from unattested Medieval Greek *πηδώτης (*pēdṓtēs, “helmsman”).
pilot.g: A person who steers a ship, a helmsman.

pin.e: From Middle English pinne, from Old English pinn (“pin, peg, bolt”), from Proto-Germanic *pinnaz, *pinnō, *pint- (“protruding point, peak, peg, pin, nail”), from Proto-Indo-European *bend- (“protruding object, pointed peg, nail, edge”).
pin.g: A needle without an eye (usually) made of drawn-out steel wire with one end sharpened and the other flattened or rounded into a head, used f

pine.e: From Middle English pyne, from Old English *pīne, from Proto-West Germanic *pīnā, from Latin pīnus, see there for more. Possibly related to fat.
pine.g: Any coniferous tree of the genus Pinus.

pine.e: From Middle English pyne, pine, probably from Old English *pīne (“pain”), from Proto-West Germanic *pīnā (“pain, torment, torture”), possibly from Latin poena (“punishment”), from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ, “penalty, fine, bloodmoney”). Entered Germanic with Christianity; cognate to Middle Dutch pinen, Old High German pīnōn, Old Norse pína.

pinion.e: From Middle English pynyon, from Old French pignon, from Latin penna (“feather”).

pinion.g: The smallest gear in a gear train.

pinnacle.e: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French pinacle, pinnacle, from Late Latin pinnāculum (“a peak, pinnacle”), from Latin pinna (“a pinnacle”); see pin.

pint.e: From Middle English pinte, from Old French pinte, assumed from Vulgar Latin *pincta (“a mark used to indicate a level of quantity against a larger measure”), from Latin picta (“painted”), from Latin pingō (“paint”, verb).
pint.g: A unit of volume, equivalent to:

pipe.e: From Middle English pīpe, pype (“hollow cylinder or tube used as a conduit or container; duct or vessel of the body; musical instrument; financial records maintained by the English Exchequer, pipe roll”), from Old English pīpe (“pipe (musical instrument); the channel of a small stream”), from Proto-West Germanic *pīpā. Reinforced by Vulgar Latin *pīpa.
pipe.g: Meanings relating to a wind instrument.

piper.e: From Middle English piper, pipere; equivalent to pipe + -er. Piecewise doublet of fifer.
piper.g: A musician who plays a pipe.

pipes.e: (vocal capacity): As if one's lungs were composed of pipework.

piss.e: From Middle English pisse (noun) and pissen (verb), from Old French pissier, possibly from Vulgar Latin *pīssiāre, probably of imitative origin.

pistachio.e: From Italian pistacchio (1590s), from Latin pistācium (“pistachio”), from Ancient Greek πιστάκιον (pistákion), from πιστάκη (pistákē, “pistachio tree”), of Iranian origin.
pistachio.g: A deciduous tree (Pistacia vera) grown in parts of Asia for its drupaceous fruit.

pit.e: From Middle English pit, pet, püt, from Old English pytt, from Proto-West Germanic *puti, from Latin puteus (“trench, pit, well”), although there are phonetic difficulties.
From Dutch pit (“kernel, core”), from Middle Dutch pitte, from Proto-Germanic *pittan (compare dialectal German Pfitze (“pimple”)), oblique of Proto-Germanic *piþō.
pit.g: A seed inside a fruit; a stone or pip inside a fruit.

pitch.e: From Middle English picche, piche, pich, from Old English piċ, from Proto-West Germanic *pik, from Latin pix.
pitch.g: A sticky, gummy substance secreted by trees; tree sap.

pitch.e: From Middle English picchen, pycchen (“to thrust in, fasten, settle”), from Old English *piċċan, from Proto-West Germanic *pikkijan, a variant of Proto-West Germanic *pikkōn (“to pick, peck”), whence Middle English pikken, picken (“to pick, pierce”), modern English pick.
pitch.g: A throw; a toss; a cast, as of something from the hand.

pitcher.g: One who pitches (in any sense) anything

pitcher.e: From Middle English picher, from Old French pichier, pechier (“small jug”), bichier (compare modern French pichet), from Late Latin or Medieval Latin pīcārium, alteration of bīcārium, itself possibly from bacarium, bacar or from Ancient Greek βῖκος (bîkos).
pitcher.g: A wide-mouthed, deep vessel for holding liquids, with a spout or protruding lip and a handle; a water jug or jar with a large ear or handle.

pitchfork.e: From Middle English pichfork, pycchefork, pychforke, pikeforke, pikkforke, pic-forcke, equivalent to pitch (verb) + fork (i.e. "a fork used for pitching or throwing material, like hay"). The figurative sense (noun sense 4) is an allusion to a crowd of farmers wielding their farm tools as weapons.
pitchfork.g: An agricultural hand tool comprising a fork with sparse, light tines, attached to a long handle, used for pitching hay (especially loose hay

pitfall.e: First recorded use in the 14th century from pit + fall in the sense of "pit trap, pit snare", from Old English fealle (“trap, snare”), from Proto-Germanic *fallą, *fallaz (“a fall, trap”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pōl-.
pitfall.g: A type of trap consisting of a concealed pit in the ground, into which the victim is supposed to fall and not be able to get out from.

pitiful.e: From Middle English pityful, piteful, piteeful. By surface analysis, pit(i) + -ful.
pitiful.g: So appalling or sad that one feels or should feel sorry for it; eliciting pity.

pity.e: From Middle English pitye, pitie, pittye, pitee, pite, from Anglo-Norman pité, pittee etc., from Old French pitet, pitié, from Latin pietās.
pity.g: A feeling of sympathy at the misfortune or suffering of someone or something.

pivot.e: From Middle English pevet, *pivot, from Old French pivot (“hinge pin, pivot”) (12th c.), possibly from Latin pūgiō.
pivot.g: A thing on which something turns; specifically a metal pointed pin or short shaft in machinery, such as the end of an axle or spindle.
